Neonates of the Namaqua dune mole-rat (Bathyergus janetta) emerge weighing just 15 grams [Wwb = 15 grams], a modest mass typical of altricial subterranean mammals. This low birth mass, approximately 4% of the adult body mass, reflects the substantial energetic constraints of a fossorial lifestyle. In a laboratory colony maintained at a constant burrow temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C], gestation was observed to last approximately 70 days [tg = approximately 70 days], a duration inferred from closely related bathyergid species and consistent with the extended gestation periods characteristic of mole-rats. The relatively prolonged gestation, combined with small litter sizes, suggests a conservative reproductive strategy adapted to the unpredictable food resources of the succulent Karoo. Following parturition, neonates are completely dependent on maternal milk and remain within the sealed natal chamber. These physiological attributes place Bathyergus janetta among the more altricial members of the rodent suborder Hystricognathi, a group already known for extended developmental timelines compared to murid rodents of equivalent body mass.

Weaning in Bathyergus janetta occurs at 28 days after birth [tx = 28 days after birth] when maintained at 34 °C [T = 34 °C], marking the transition from exclusive milk ingestion to the consumption of solid plant material. This weaning age, while longer than in many surface-dwelling rodents of comparable birth mass, is relatively short for a hystricognath species, likely reflecting the selective pressure for accelerated independence in an energetically demanding burrow environment. During the nursing stage, the mother provisions the developing pup with lipid-rich milk that supports rapid early growth. The timing of weaning coincides with the point at which juvenile animals can begin to process geophytes, the primary dietary component of this species. Field observations suggest that weaned juveniles remain within the maternal burrow system for several additional weeks, gradually learning to locate and excavate underground storage organs before dispersing to establish their own territories. This extended period of post-weaning association contrasts with the abrupt independence observed in many muroid rodents.

Sexual maturation in captive Namaqua dune mole-rats occurs at 365 days after birth [tp = 365 days after birth] under standard thermal conditions of 34 °C [T = 34 °C], a milestone that represents the transition from the juvenile to the adult reproductive stage. This relatively late onset of puberty, equivalent to approximately 6% of the species' maximum lifespan, is characteristic of bathyergid rodents and reflect their slow life-history pace. The delay in reproductive activation is thought to be mediated by social cues and body condition, as subordinate individuals in wild colonies may defer maturation further. Histological examination of gonadal tissue confirms that gametogenesis commences at this age, with testicular descent and first oestrus occurring within a narrow temporal window. This developmental schedule, substantially slower than that of above-ground rodents of equivalent body size, underscores the metabolic constraints imposed by a subterranean habitat where food availability is patchy and burrowing is energetically costly. The age at first reproduction in free-living individuals may be delayed relative to laboratory values due to ecological limitations.

The maximum lifespan recorded for captive Bathyergus janetta reaches 16 years [am = 16 years] at a burrow temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C], a remarkably long duration for a rodent of its body size and one that aligns with the extended longevity documented across the Bathyergidae. This extreme longevity, exceeding 5,840 days, is associated with a slow aging rate and sustained reproductive capacity well into advanced age. At the terminal stage of the life cycle, individuals exhibit gradual physiological decline characterized by dental wear, reduced locomotor activity, and diminished sensory function. The ultimate adult body mass attained by reproductively active individuals is approximately 390 grams [Wwi = approximately 390 grams], with males typically reaching slightly larger dimensions than females. This asymptotic body mass, representing the maximum size achieved after growth ceases, is modest compared to the congeneric giant mole-rat (Bathyergus suillus) but substantial relative to other members of the Bathyerginae subfamily. The combination of small litters, delayed reproduction, and extreme longevity places Bathyergus janetta at the slow end of the mammalian life-history continuum.

Female Namaqua dune mole-rats produce approximately 7 pups per year [Ri = approximately 7 pups per year] when maintained under stable thermal conditions at 34 °C [T = 34 °C]. This low annual fecundity is among the lowest recorded for hystricognath rodents and reflects the species' energy-conserving reproductive strategy. The peak fertility is achieved during the rainy season when succulent geophytes are most abundant and soil conditions are optimal for excavation. Reproductive output is highly sensitive to environmental variation, with captive colonies demonstrating that females in poor body condition may skip breeding seasons entirely. Data from field populations indicate that mortality during the first year of life is substantial, and only a fraction of weaned pups survive to reach the 365-day threshold of puberty (365 days after birth) [tp = 365 days after birth] at a temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C].
